subject: embedded
title: Firmware and Microcontroller Foundations
summary: Understand what firmware controls, how microcontrollers use memory and peripherals, how to read board documentation, and how a build reaches a running main loop.

lessons.title: What embedded software does
lessons.summary: Identify the inputs, decisions, outputs and constraints of a small firmware system.
lessons.body:
A room sensor reads a measurement, decides whether a threshold has been crossed and changes an indicator. The program has the familiar ingredients of any software system: data, conditions, functions and state. What changes is its relationship with the physical device.

**Embedded software** runs as part of a device's particular purpose. **Firmware** is the software stored for that device to execute, often in memory that retains its contents without power. The term does not mean that the software can never be updated. The vendor's supported update process determines how a particular device changes its firmware.

This course concentrates on small **microcontrollers**, or MCUs. You can learn their software structure and test decision logic on a computer before choosing a development board.

## Start with behaviour

For an illustrative sensor indicator, write the behaviour before writing code:

| Part | Example requirement |
|---|---|
| Input | A new measurement and whether it is valid |
| Decision | Compare a valid measurement with a limit |
| Output | Update the indicator |
| Fault | Show a distinct indication when data is invalid |

The threshold and the fault indication are choices for this example, not universal sensor rules. A first useful test is a sequence of inputs: below the threshold, above it, then invalid. The expected outputs are normal, alert, then fault. That sequence can be tested without connecting an actual sensor.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a receptionist following a procedure
> A receptionist receives information, checks a rule and gives an appropriate response. If the information is missing, the procedure can specify a different response.
>
> **How it maps:** Incoming information represents sensor input, the rule represents firmware logic and the response represents an output. An explicit missing-information rule represents fault handling.
>
> **Where it stops:** A microcontroller cannot use human judgement to fill in an omitted rule. Firmware must define its inputs, timing and failure behaviour precisely.

## What changes from desktop development

A **bare-metal** application runs without an operating system managing its application execution. Its startup code and libraries still do real work. A real-time operating system is still an operating system; an application running under one is not bare metal. Other embedded devices use an operating system, so embedded does not automatically mean bare metal.

Hardware places constraints on available memory, supported signals and the time allowed for a response. A **real-time** requirement concerns meeting a timing requirement, not simply running as fast as possible. A program that eventually gives the right answer can still fail if that answer arrives too late for its intended job.

For this course's small project, success means the logic is correct, operations return control promptly, and invalid input has a defined outcome. Later modules add device interfaces and timing methods to that foundation.

## Key takeaways
- Describe observable inputs, decisions, outputs and fault behaviour before choosing implementation details.
- Firmware can be updateable; embedded systems can run with or without an operating system.
- Correct timing can be part of correct behaviour.

## Further reading
- [Firmware definitions — NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/firmware)
- [Bare metal excludes an OS or RTOS — Altera](https://www.altera.com/developers/embedded-software/bare-metal)
- [Pico microcontroller boards — Raspberry Pi](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/microcontrollers/pico-series/about_pico.adoc)
- [RP2040 datasheet: system description](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf)

questions.prompt: A sensor indicator must show normal, alert or fault. Which is the most useful first description of its software behaviour?

options.text: Choose a fast MCU before deciding what a fault means.
options.explanation: Processor choice does not define the observable behaviour or failure response.

options.text: List its inputs, decisions, outputs and invalid-input response.
options.explanation: Correct. These define behaviour that can be traced and tested before adding hardware details.

options.text: Assume every measurement is valid until hardware exists.
options.explanation: Invalid measurements are a behaviour case, so omitting them leaves the fault response undefined.

options.text: Use firmware so the program cannot be changed later.
options.explanation: Firmware is not inherently unchangeable; update support depends on the device and its programming process.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify the measurement and its validity as inputs.
2. Define the output for a valid value below the threshold.
3. Define the output above the threshold.
4. Define a separate output for invalid data. This produces a small testable behaviour specification.

questions.prompt: An appropriate Pico firmware image is copied using the documented BOOTSEL workflow. What does this illustrate about firmware?

options.text: Firmware must be a desktop process.
options.explanation: The image runs on the board; a desktop application can transfer it without turning it into a desktop process.

options.text: Firmware always requires an operating system.
options.explanation: The update mechanism does not establish an operating-system requirement.

options.text: Firmware can only be read, never replaced.
options.explanation: The documented programming workflow replaces the executable image on supported storage.

options.text: A device can support updating its stored firmware.
options.explanation: Correct. The official programming process supplies an update route; this does not mean all devices use the same route.

questions.workedExample:
1. Source or a supplied binary describes the new program.
2. The supported programming interface transfers that image.
3. The device can then execute the changed image. Firmware describes its role in the device, not a promise that updates are impossible.

questions.prompt: Which statements fit the scope of a beginner embedded application? Select all that apply.

options.text: A response may need to arrive within a specified time.
options.explanation: Correct. A timing requirement can be part of the required behaviour.

options.text: Embedded software always means no operating system.
options.explanation: Bare-metal is one arrangement; embedded systems can also use an operating system.

options.text: The decision logic can be tested with invented input sequences on a computer.
options.explanation: Correct. Such tests check the logic while leaving physical signals and hardware timing to other checks.

options.text: Correct results eventually are enough for every use.
options.explanation: If the use has a timing requirement, arriving too late can be a failure even when the value is right.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the decision rule from the physical input mechanism.
2. Exercise below-limit, above-limit and invalid-data cases with test inputs.
3. Treat any specified response time as another requirement. A computer-only test of the decisions does not prove hardware timing.

lessons.title: CPU, memory and peripherals
lessons.summary: Separate instruction execution, persistent storage, working memory and hardware interfaces.
lessons.body:
A **microcontroller** combines one or more processor cores, memory and hardware interfaces in a chip. The exact mixture varies. The development board around it may add more memory, power circuitry, connectors and other components.

The **CPU**, or central processing unit, executes instructions. It uses **RAM**, random-access memory, for working data such as changing variables and temporary buffers. The SRAM commonly used by small MCUs is **volatile memory**: its contents are not retained when power is removed.

**Flash memory** is non-volatile storage that can hold firmware and persistent data. It may be inside the MCU or on a separate chip. As a concrete distinction, RP2040 has on-chip SRAM and accesses external flash through its flash interface. Do not assume that a board's advertised flash capacity describes memory inside its processor.

## Give each part a job

For the sensor indicator introduced earlier:

| Part | Job in the example |
|---|---|
| CPU | Execute the measurement decision |
| Firmware storage | Retain the program when power is removed |
| RAM | Hold the current measurement and state |
| Peripheral | Exchange signals with the sensor or indicator |

A **peripheral** is a dedicated hardware block such as a timer or a serial controller. Software configures it and observes or supplies data. The peripheral can perform its configured hardware work between CPU instructions; it does not decide the application's requirements for you.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a workshop with instructions and a workbench
> A workshop keeps instructions in a cupboard, places the current job on a workbench and uses specialised tools for particular operations.
>
> **How it maps:** Stored instructions represent firmware storage; the workbench represents working RAM; the worker following instructions represents the CPU. Specialised tools represent peripherals.
>
> **Where it stops:** Actual memory has defined addresses and access rules. Some systems execute code from RAM, and a peripheral's registers are not ordinary storage just because software accesses them by address.

## Addresses describe different kinds of access

A **memory map** describes which addresses refer to memory and which refer to hardware. A **peripheral register** is a location used to control or observe a hardware function. For example, one register can select a pin's function while another reports an input value.

Access can cause **register side effects**: reading or writing a peripheral register is not automatically equivalent to reading or writing a RAM variable. Later lessons use the relevant device manual or SDK rather than guessing addresses.

Try a mental power cycle. The saved firmware can remain in flash, but the current working measurement is not a persistent record merely because it was stored in RAM. To retain a setting, the application needs an appropriate supported storage mechanism and a defined loading process.

## Key takeaways
- Distinguish firmware storage from the RAM used while the program runs.
- MCU and board memory are different descriptions; check the actual device.
- Peripherals and their registers have device-specific behaviour.

## Further reading
- [RP2040 datasheet: memory and peripheral descriptions](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf)
- [Pico board memory and storage — Raspberry Pi](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/microcontrollers/pico-series/about_pico.adoc)

questions.prompt: A program stores the latest measurement only in the ordinary volatile working RAM used in this example. Power is removed. What should its design assume?

options.text: That measurement is not a persistent record.
options.explanation: Correct. Volatile working memory does not provide retention through power removal.

options.text: The CPU automatically writes it to flash before power disappears.
options.explanation: No automatic saving mechanism was specified; retention needs an explicit supported design.

options.text: It will return because the firmware image remains in flash.
options.explanation: Retaining instructions and retaining the latest working data are separate requirements.

options.text: Every peripheral retains a duplicate copy.
options.explanation: Peripheral behaviour is device-specific; no persistent duplicate was defined.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify where the measurement was stored: volatile working RAM.
2. Distinguish that data from the firmware retained in non-volatile storage.
3. If the measurement must survive power loss, add an appropriate storage and loading mechanism rather than assuming retention.

questions.prompt: A development board advertises flash memory. Which question avoids confusing the board with its MCU?

options.text: Does the word flash prove that all code executes from RAM?
options.explanation: Flash capacity does not determine the execution path.

options.text: Can RAM replace the need for any startup code?
options.explanation: Memory availability alone does not establish how execution begins.

options.text: Is that flash inside the MCU or connected as a separate component?
options.explanation: Correct. RP2040 is an example where external flash and on-chip SRAM have different roles.

options.text: Does advertised capacity prove every address is writable like a RAM variable?
options.explanation: Access permissions and register side effects come from the actual memory map and device documentation.

questions.workedExample:
1. Read the chip memory description.
2. Read the board memory and wiring description.
3. Identify the physical storage component and how it is accessed. A board specification may include components outside the MCU package.

questions.prompt: Why should a peripheral register not be treated as an arbitrary RAM location?

options.text: Registers cannot have addresses.
options.explanation: Memory-mapped peripherals are reached through addresses; their behaviour is the important difference.

options.text: A register read or write can control hardware or have another documented side effect.
options.explanation: Correct. A register is a hardware interface whose documented access behaviour matters.

options.text: Every register permanently stores configuration after power removal.
options.explanation: Persistence is not implied by being a peripheral register.

options.text: The CPU never accesses peripheral registers.
options.explanation: Software can configure or observe peripherals through the documented register or SDK interface.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ordinary RAM holds working values.
2. A peripheral register can control a function or report device state.
3. Therefore check the documented access semantics before assuming that an ordinary read-modify-write sequence is appropriate.

lessons.title: Read the chip, board and SDK documentation
lessons.summary: Use the chip datasheet, board wiring and SDK configuration together before controlling a pin.
lessons.body:
An example says it blinks an LED, but your board stays dark. Before changing code at random, distinguish three sources of information.

The **datasheet** describes a component: its supported functions, electrical limits, registers and required operating conditions. A board manual and **schematic** describe how a particular circuit board connects those components. The **SDK**, or software development kit, supplies libraries, header files, examples and build support for a supported target.

None replaces the others. A chip may support a function on several pins, while the board uses one of those pins for another purpose. A library may also require a specific board selection so it chooses the correct implementation.

## Work from the device outward

For an onboard indicator, follow this sequence:

1. Identify the exact board model and revision, not just the processor family.
2. Read its manual or schematic to find how the indicator is connected.
3. Check which component controls that connection.
4. Use the official SDK example for that board and check its build configuration.
5. Observe the intended result before adding external circuitry.

The Raspberry Pi SDK's blink example illustrates why this matters. Its ordinary Pico LED path and Pico W wireless-chip LED path differ. The example selects the supported path using board configuration. Copying a pin number from a different board is not a substitute for that selection.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: an appliance manual and a room plan
> An appliance manual explains what the appliance can do. A room plan shows where it is installed and how it is connected. A control panel provides the supported way to operate it.
>
> **How it maps:** The component datasheet describes the device's capabilities, the board schematic describes actual connections and the SDK provides a software interface to those capabilities.
>
> **Where it stops:** A board's connections can constrain what is usable. Neither a convenient API nor a familiar connector overrides the component's electrical limits or the board's wiring.

## Keep the first experiment simple

Use a board's documented onboard indicator for the first hardware observation. If an example builds but does not work, check the selected board, the actual firmware image loaded and the documented indicator connection before concluding the MCU is broken.

Keep any later experiments to low-voltage development hardware. Before connecting an external signal, check the electrical limits for inputs, ground reference and power arrangement in the exact manuals. Do not connect unknown voltage sources or high-current loads directly to MCU pins. This course does not require external wiring to understand or test its first logic examples.

## Key takeaways
- A component's capabilities, a board's connections and an SDK's configuration answer different questions.
- Match an example to the exact board before assuming a particular pin controls its indicator.
- Electrical limits remain hardware requirements even when an API accepts a value.

## Further reading
- [SDK board selection and first examples — Raspberry Pi](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/microcontrollers/c_sdk/official_sdk.adoc)
- [Official blink implementation — Raspberry Pi](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-examples/master/blink/blink.c)
- [RP2040 datasheet](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf)

questions.prompt: An SDK blink example builds but the indicator stays dark on a different board variant. What should you check first?

options.text: Increase the pin drive without reading limits.
options.explanation: Electrical changes without the correct device limits are not a valid diagnostic step.

options.text: Assume all onboard LEDs share a CPU pin.
options.explanation: The official Pico example includes different paths for supported board variants.

options.text: Replace the MCU because compilation succeeded.
options.explanation: A successful build does not prove the correct board or indicator connection was selected.

options.text: Check the exact board, indicator connection and SDK board selection.
options.explanation: Correct. The component, board and build configuration must describe the same intended target.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify the exact board model.
2. Find how its indicator is connected.
3. Confirm that the official example and board selection support that connection.
4. Confirm the matching image was loaded before investigating a hardware fault.

questions.prompt: Which document is the appropriate starting point for finding how a board connector is wired to its components?

options.text: The board manual or schematic.
options.explanation: Correct. These describe the actual board connections, which may use only some chip capabilities.

options.text: A compiler warning list.
options.explanation: Compiler diagnostics do not describe the physical board wiring.

options.text: A source example for any board with the same processor.
options.explanation: A shared processor does not imply identical connections.

options.text: The application behaviour specification alone.
options.explanation: The specification defines intended behaviour, not the physical routes on a manufactured board.

questions.workedExample:
1. The datasheet describes the component.
2. The schematic describes the board connections.
3. The SDK configuration selects a supported software target. To locate a connector connection, start with the board documentation.

link.title: Board documentation and schematics — Raspberry Pi

questions.prompt: Which statements are valid when preparing a first hardware experiment? Select all that apply.

options.text: An API accepting a number guarantees the electrical connection is safe.
options.explanation: Software argument acceptance does not override electrical limits or board wiring.

options.text: An onboard indicator can provide an initial documented observation without external signal wiring.
options.explanation: Correct. It gives a simple observation point when used through the exact board guide.

options.text: External signals need their voltage and ground-reference requirements checked in the exact manuals.
options.explanation: Correct. Compatibility is a hardware requirement, not an assumption derived from a familiar connector.

options.text: An unknown voltage source is suitable if its connector fits.
options.explanation: A matching connector does not establish electrical compatibility.

questions.workedExample:
1. Begin with the documented onboard output.
2. Match the SDK example to that board.
3. Before adding external signals, check the actual interface limits, power arrangement and reference. Do not connect unknown voltage sources directly to MCU pins.

link.title: Debug connections and ground-reference precautions — Raspberry Pi

lessons.title: From source code to a running device
lessons.summary: Distinguish compiling, linking, transferring firmware and observing its behaviour.
lessons.body:
Writing a source file changes a file on your computer. It does not change the program already running on a board. A firmware workflow must turn that source into an appropriate image, transfer it using a supported method and then observe what actually runs.

A **toolchain** is the collection of development tools used for that target. A **cross-compiler** runs on one system while producing code for another target. Choosing the wrong target can produce perfectly valid machine code that the intended MCU cannot execute.

## Follow the stages

This is a simplified development sequence, not a set of shell commands:

```flow
Edit the source
Compile target object files
Link the firmware image
Transfer it using the supported tool
Reset or start the application
Observe the required behaviour
```

The **compiler** translates source into target code, often producing **object files**. In a C toolchain, preprocessing handles items such as header inclusion before compilation proper. The **linker** combines object files and libraries, resolves references between them and lays out the result according to the target's build configuration.

A successful compile does not prove that linking will succeed. A function can have a declaration that allows compilation while its implementation is missing from the link. Similarly, successful linking does not prove that the resulting program satisfies the device's behaviour requirements.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: preparing and delivering a printed instruction pack
> Different people prepare pages, someone assembles the complete pack, and a delivery step takes it to the place where it will be used. Finishing a page does not prove the pack was delivered or followed correctly.
>
> **How it maps:** Preparing pages represents compilation; assembling the pack represents linking; delivery represents transferring the firmware. Observing the device checks the behaviour of the delivered result.
>
> **Where it stops:** Firmware must match a processor, memory layout and transfer format. A successfully delivered image can still contain logical errors or initialise the wrong hardware.

## A concrete supported route

For an original Raspberry Pi Pico running an appropriate Pico SDK blink image, the official documentation describes entering BOOTSEL mode, which exposes a USB mass-storage interface, then copying a UF2 image through that interface. The bootloader interprets the transfer and the board restarts into the application. This is a Pico workflow, not a universal way of programming MCUs or an ordinary storage drive for arbitrary files.

Other supported routes use a debug interface and a programming tool. Follow the board's current guide for the required image format and procedure. Record the board selection, build configuration and image you transferred so an observation can be tied to a particular build.

## Key takeaways
- Build, transfer and observation are separate steps; success at one does not prove success at the next.
- A cross-compiler and linker must target the actual device and build configuration.
- Use an official board-specific programming method rather than assuming all MCUs accept the same file.

## Further reading
- [Overall compilation and linking options — GCC](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Overall-Options.html)
- [First binaries and BOOTSEL workflow — Raspberry Pi](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/microcontrollers/c_sdk/your_first_binary.adoc)
- [Debug probe programming and debugging — Raspberry Pi](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/microcontrollers/debug-probe/introduction.adoc)

questions.prompt: A C source file compiles, but linking reports that a referenced function has no implementation in the build. Which stage has not yet succeeded?

options.text: Source editing only.
options.explanation: Editing occurred, but the reported failure belongs to the stage combining the translated program parts.

options.text: Flashing after a successful image.
options.explanation: There is no successfully linked image from this build yet.

options.text: Linking the object files and libraries.
options.explanation: Correct. A declaration can permit compilation even though no linked object supplies the required function definition.

options.text: The physical indicator test only.
options.explanation: The program has not reached the later hardware-observation stage.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compilation can translate a call when the function is declared.
2. The linker must then find the implementation among the included objects and libraries.
3. A missing implementation prevents the final image from being linked; diagnose the build before flashing.

questions.prompt: You edit a source file but do not build or transfer anything. What has changed on a board already running an older image?

options.text: Its flash immediately contains the edited text.
options.explanation: Source editing on the host is not a programming operation on the target.

options.text: Nothing about its running image follows from that edit alone.
options.explanation: Correct. Building and transferring the intended image are separate required steps.

options.text: Its runtime starts using the host source automatically.
options.explanation: The described firmware workflow provides no live source-loading mechanism.

options.text: Its processor automatically changes target architecture.
options.explanation: Target architecture is a hardware and toolchain choice, not an effect of saving source.

questions.workedExample:
1. Saving changes the source file on the host.
2. Building creates the target artefacts.
3. Transferring the supported image changes what is available on the device. Keep these steps distinct when interpreting an observation.

questions.prompt: After a successful image transfer, which checks help establish that the intended application is running correctly? Select all that apply.

options.text: Whether the application produces the specified behaviour.
options.explanation: Correct. A transfer result is not a functional test.

options.text: Whether the build selected the intended board configuration.
options.explanation: Correct. A transferred image can still be for an unintended configuration.

options.text: Whether every MCU uses UF2.
options.explanation: No such conclusion follows. UF2 programming is a supported route for particular devices, not a universal MCU rule.

options.text: Skip input tests because the transfer proves every logical requirement.
options.explanation: A successful transfer does not exercise the required input-to-output behaviour, so input tests must not be skipped for that reason.

questions.workedExample:
1. Tie the transferred image to its recorded board and build configuration.
2. Start or reset it as documented.
3. Observe the specified outputs and test the defined input cases. Programming success and behaviour correctness are separate checks.

lessons.title: From reset to application startup
lessons.summary: Trace a documented reset path without assuming every MCU begins directly at main.
lessons.body:
Resetting a device is not the same operation as flashing new firmware. A **reset** restarts execution through a defined hardware and software path. Programming flash changes stored contents. Either operation may be part of a development tool's sequence, but one does not automatically imply the other.

Your application's first visible action may be turning an indicator on. Before that action, the processor and its support code need a way to locate executable code and establish an environment in which that code can run.

## Trace one documented startup model

Arm's CMSIS Cortex-M startup template describes a **reset handler**, an initial **stack pointer**, and an **interrupt vector table** containing handler addresses. The reset handler typically calls system initialisation, then transfers control to a C runtime that performs its initialisation and calls the application's `main` function. Here `main` is the entry function used by that runtime; it is not the first instruction executed after reset.

This names a particular Cortex-M software model. The exact sequence comes from the chip, toolchain and project. Another processor or startup package can use a different arrangement.

C variables with **static storage duration** have storage for the whole program execution; program-wide variables are an example. C requires these variables to receive their initial values before C program startup. The described runtime completes this initialisation before calling `main`. This is a software initialisation rule, not a claim that reset hardware erases all physical RAM. C does not require every microcontroller project to use an entry function named `main`.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: opening a shop before serving customers
> A shop can need its entrance opened, workspace prepared and equipment checked before the first customer is served.
>
> **How it maps:** The opening procedure represents the reset and startup path; serving the first customer represents entering application code. A fault during preparation can prevent the application's first visible action.
>
> **Where it stops:** There is no universal startup checklist for every MCU. Hardware-defined entry rules and vendor startup code determine the real order, and a reset need not erase every memory region.

## Boot code and application code are distinct

A **bootloader** is code that loads or starts another program and may support a programming or recovery interface. Some devices begin in manufacturer **ROM**, read-only memory containing fixed boot code. Others enter an application image more directly. These arrangements are device-specific.

RP2040 is one concrete example: its boot ROM participates in startup and supports the documented USB boot interface. That example should not be expanded into a claim that every MCU has a USB bootloader.

When diagnosing a board that never reaches the application, ask which milestone failed. Did the programming tool report a successful transfer? Can the debug tools reach the target? Does execution reach application startup? Does hardware initialisation finish? These observations separate a startup failure from a failure in the later decision logic.

Treat retained settings deliberately. Some reset conditions can preserve physical RAM or special retention storage, while startup code may reinitialise application data. Check the specific device and runtime rather than using a reset as a general promise to erase all data.

## Key takeaways
- Reset, flash programming, startup and application entry are distinct operations.
- `main` is reached through supporting code in the described CMSIS startup model.
- Boot behaviour and retention depend on the target and its startup configuration.

## Further reading
- [Cortex-M startup file and reset handler — Arm CMSIS](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS_6/latest/Core/startup_c_pg.html)
- [System initialisation — Arm CMSIS](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS_6/latest/Core/group__system__init__gr.html)
- [C11 draft: execution environments, sections 5.1.2 and 5.1.2.1](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [RP2040 datasheet: boot sequence](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf)

questions.prompt: In the CMSIS Cortex-M startup template described in the lesson, which preparation normally precedes the application main function?

options.text: A reset handler and runtime establish the documented startup environment.
options.explanation: Correct. The template describes reset handling, system initialisation and transfer to the runtime before main.

options.text: The application main function chooses its own first reset instruction.
options.explanation: The reset path exists before the application entry function is called.

options.text: Every RAM address is necessarily erased by the reset hardware.
options.explanation: Retention and startup initialisation are device- and runtime-specific.

options.text: A new firmware image must be downloaded on every reset.
options.explanation: Reset restarts execution; it does not inherently require programming a new image.

questions.workedExample:
1. The processor enters the documented reset path.
2. In this CMSIS template the reset handler normally calls system initialisation.
3. Control passes to the C runtime, which performs its initialisation and calls main. This describes the template, not a universal startup sequence for every architecture.

questions.prompt: Why is resetting a board different from flashing it?

options.text: Reset always removes its non-volatile program.
options.explanation: Restarting execution does not inherently erase or replace stored program contents.

options.text: Flashing only changes variables already in working RAM.
options.explanation: Flash programming concerns supported non-volatile storage, not just current RAM variables.

options.text: Both words mean exactly the same operation on every target.
options.explanation: A tool can perform both in one workflow, but their purposes remain different.

options.text: Reset restarts execution; flashing programs stored contents through a supported method.
options.explanation: Correct. A programming tool may subsequently reset the target, but the actions are distinct.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify the action being requested.
2. Programming changes stored contents.
3. Reset follows the defined startup path. A workflow may combine them, so record which part succeeded rather than treating one success message as proof of both.

questions.prompt: A board never reaches the application first indicator update. Which investigation best separates startup from application logic?

options.text: Assume a USB bootloader exists because another MCU has one.
options.explanation: Boot support is device-specific; it cannot be inferred from an unrelated target.

options.text: Change every threshold in the sensor decision.
options.explanation: If execution never reaches the application, changing later decisions does not identify the failing milestone.

options.text: Check transfer results, debug access and whether execution reaches application startup.
options.explanation: Correct. These observations locate milestones before the later indicator logic.

options.text: Assume an unlit indicator proves flash is empty.
options.explanation: The output can fail for several reasons, including configuration or startup, so this is not a sufficient diagnosis.

questions.workedExample:
1. Confirm what the programming tool actually reported.
2. Use supported debug observations to locate execution.
3. Check whether application startup and hardware initialisation are reached. Only then interpret the later input-to-output logic.

lessons.title: Keep a main loop responsive with explicit state
lessons.summary: Trace bounded main-loop work and distinguish a button state from a new button event.
lessons.body:
A **main loop**, sometimes called a superloop, repeatedly performs the application's foreground work. In a **cooperative** design, each operation returns control so the loop can visit its other jobs. One operation that waits indefinitely can prevent all later foreground jobs from running.

An explicit **state machine** records the current mode and defines how an input changes it. It replaces vague instructions such as "handle the button somehow" with a rule that can be traced and tested.

## Separate an event from a level

For this teaching example, a button toggles an indicator between OFF and ON. The input is an already accepted press event, not the raw electrical signal and not a button-held level. The later debounce lesson explains how to derive such events from real input.

This is illustrative pseudocode, not C or an SDK API. Each input check and output update is assumed to return promptly. The assignments initialise or change the remembered state.

```text
state <- OFF
repeat:
  event <- take_one_press_event()
  if event is PRESS:
    if state is OFF:
      state <- ON
    else:
      state <- OFF
  apply_indicator(state)
  service_other_work()
```

One loop pass consumes at most one event. With an initial state of OFF, the sequence below gives a deterministic trace:

| Pass | Accepted event | State after pass |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | none | OFF |
| 2 | PRESS | ON |
| 3 | none, button still held | ON |
| 4 | PRESS after another press | OFF |

Using the held-button level as the event would toggle again on every pass while the button stayed down. A fast loop would then produce behaviour unrelated to the number of deliberate presses.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: one person checking several service desks
> A person visits several desks in order, handles a small piece of work at each and returns for the next round. Waiting forever at one desk prevents visits to the others.
>
> **How it maps:** The person represents foreground execution, desks represent loop jobs and each short visit represents work that returns control. The remembered indicator mode represents the application's explicit state.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real MCU interrupts can run between foreground instructions, and another core may run simultaneously. A loop structure alone proves neither a response-time limit nor safe access to shared data.

## Test decisions separately from hardware

The event-to-state rule can be tested on a computer with a list of input events. That checks the defined transitions; it does not validate the physical button, signal levels or output wiring.

To reason about responsiveness, list the maximum work each foreground job can do before returning. Avoid an unbounded wait for input inside a loop job. Later timing and debugging lessons add elapsed-time scheduling, bounded communication and observation methods. They also explain why merely adding interrupts or more scheduling machinery does not establish a timing guarantee.

## Key takeaways
- Cooperative jobs must return control for the loop to service other foreground work.
- Remember explicit state and consume an accepted event once.
- A trace can test decision logic without claiming to validate hardware or deadlines.
